newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico army returns to barracks before state vote.
newsitem.headline: Mexico army returns to barracks before state vote.

text.p: Mexican troops have temporarily suspended counter-insurgency operations in the western state of Guerrero and returned to their barracks ahead of state elections on Sunday, officials said on Saturday.
Thousands of army troops in the violence-plagued state will keep to the sidelines during Sunday's vote to elect new mayors and a new state congress, said Roberto Alvarez, a state spokesman.
"The army will not be visible in any part of the election process. They will keep to their barracks, but of course will be on alert for any incidents," Alvarez told Reuters.
Local media reported that troops were still patrolling some remote towns on Friday, although no troops were visible in the state capital Chilpancingo, some 220 miles (350 km) south of Mexico City.

The move could help ease tension in the state following allegations by opposition parties that the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) was using dirty tricks such as vote-buying to win the race. Acting State Gov. Angel Aguirre has promised to investigate the allegations.

The suspension of military activity also comes after a new guerrilla group in the region, the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR), recently called a unilateral ceasefire before the elections, which are expected to benefit the PRI.
Human rights groups have expressed concern a massive troop presence in Guerrero could keep some voters from the polls.

Human rights groups estimate there are some 15,000 troops in the state right now, most of which poured in during the summer months in search of EPR guerrillas, who have launched sporadic attacks against the army here and in other central states.

"Political violence in the state, the army, and the EPR have together created a climate of fear among the population here which has already hurt this election," said David Fernandez, the head of Miguel Agustin Pro human rights group.

Alianza Civica, another Mexican human rights group, said it will have 300 electoral observers on hand for the vote. It said its observers have already documented irregularities by local officials of the PRI, which has ruled Mexico for 67 years.

In the town of Xalpatlahuac, a remote mountain hamlet some 200 miles (340 km) south of Mexico City, PRI officials were promising would-be voters free bags of government cement, according to Alianza Civica.
"Unfortunately, there have been serious irregularities due to vote buying and intimidation," Martha Perez, a member of Alianza's executive committee, told reporters on Saturday.
